newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenyan millers seek alternative to coffee auctions.
newsitem.headline: Kenyan millers seek alternative to coffee auctions.

text.p: Kenyan coffee millers said on Monday they were seeking an option to sell other than through a central auction, to encourage competition and transparency.

Top executives from Kenya Planters' Cooperative Union (KPCU) and Thika Coffee Mills said they wanted the auction system to be retained but the government to give them an option to sell coffee outside the auction if that provided better prices.
They said they planned to withhold milled coffee to force the Coffee Board of Kenya (CBK) to agree to their demand for licensing of other companies to join the board in marketing.
CBK reported shortages in coffee delivery from mills which was expected to put further pressure on prices at auction. But officials did not quantify the shortages with figures.
Under Kenyan law, millers hand over all processed coffee to the CBK which sells it at the export auction and passes on payments directly to farmers. CBK pays miller charges directly.
The millers say it is ridiculous to hand over milled coffee to the board, then purchase it at the auction for their clients. They say they should have direct authority to market coffee.
Board Managing Director James Nyaga and Thika Coffee Mills Chairman Pius Ngugi said they were concerned that the CBK played a regulatory role and was also the sole coffee marketing agent.
"Millers would like to introduce a system that will create transparency and accountability and offer checks and balances within the central auction," Ngugi told a news conference.

"Central auctions will always be there. We seek an option to sell outside the auction if prices offered are higher than those attained at the auction. That will be done with regulatory supervision. Nothing is outside the system," Nyaga said.
"We'll go to the auctions if the prices are right. But we should sell to roasters directly if they offer better prices, the farmers can only benefit with that option," Nyaga added.

This month, President Daniel arap Moi appeared to signal a change in policy, saying millers would be allowed an influential marketing role provided they raised one billion shillings ($18 million) as bail protection against any farmer losses.
But in an unexpected turnaround Moi later said coffee marketing lay under the sole authority of the coffee board and no one should interfere with that mandate.
The millers said coffee traders favoured a central export auction because it gave them more control over prices. Leading traders in Nairobi rejected that suggestion.
KPCU and Thika Coffee Mills have taken their campaign to end coffee marketing dominance by the board to key growing areas.
KPCU mills around 70 percent of Kenya's total coffee production while Thika Coffee Mills process 10 percent.
Production is estimated at 78,000 tonnes in 1996/97.
